summary: This informational document defines a methodology for measuring how long a network forwarding device takes to resume forwarding after a reset. It covers different reset types, such as software and hardware restarts. The aim is to make results from different devices comparable for benchmarking.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6201 gives testers a consistent way to measure how long a network device stops forwarding after a reset. It defines two measurement methods and describes tests for hardware, software, and power events.

subtitle: A repeatable way to measure how long forwarding stops during a device reset.

tldr.problem: A forwarding device may stop forwarding during a reset, and different reset types and device designs make recovery time difficult to compare.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines reset time, gives frame-loss and timestamp measurement methods, and sets test procedures for hardware resets, software resets, and power interruption.
tldr.outcome: The methodology updates RFC 2544, and its definition of reset time updates RFC 1242. The document is Informational.

facts.label: Power interruption
facts.value: At least 15 seconds; subtract 15 seconds in reporting

today: RFC 6201 is an Informational RFC published in March 2011. The unit metadata says it updates RFC 1242 and RFC 2544, and lists no later update or obsoleting RFC.

sections.title: Definition of Reset Time
sections.content:
A reset is a restart of a forwarding device or one of its components. The device may stop forwarding frames during the reset and recovery. The RFC defines reset time as the total time the device is out of operation, including both the reset itself and recovery.

The measurement is reported in milliseconds. Software upgrades are outside the document's scope. RFC 6201 updates Section 26.6 of RFC 2544 and updates the benchmarking term in RFC 1242.
sections.plainLanguage: Reset time measures how long a device cannot forward traffic while it resets and recovers. The measure includes the reset event and the time until forwarding resumes.

sections.title: Two Ways to Measure the Interruption
sections.content:
The frame-loss method divides the number of lost frames by the offered frame rate. It requires a test tool that can count lost frames and a known transmission rate. The timestamp method records the time of the last frame received before the interruption and the first frame received after it; their difference is the reset time.

The tester may use either method, depending on the tool. The RFC recommends frame loss when the tool can count loss per stream and transmit regardless of link status. It recommends timestamps when the tool can timestamp each frame and sends only while the link is up. If both methods are available, the tester should use the more accurate one.
sections.plainLanguage: A tester can count missing frames and use the sending rate to estimate the interruption. Or the tester can compare the arrival times of the last frame before the reset and the first frame after it.

sections.title: Test Conditions and Result Reporting
sections.content:
For a fair comparison, the tester MUST use identical control-plane and data-plane information across devices and report factors that may affect recovery. These factors include the reset type, whether it is manual or automatic, scheduled or not, local or remote, and the scale and redundancy of the device.

Reports include reset time and frame loss, if measured. The RFC recommends reporting throughput, average loss, average reset time, number of trials, protocol, frame size, port media, port speed, and encapsulation. Multiple trials and an average result are recommended. If no frames are lost, the report says “no loss.”
sections.plainLanguage: Run comparable tests with the same traffic and settings, and record details that can affect recovery. Report the measured interruption and enough test information for another person to understand the result.

sections.title: Hardware, Software, and Power Tests
sections.content:
The RFC covers hardware resets, software resets, and complete power interruption. Hardware cases include resetting a routing processor or removing and reinserting a line card. Software cases include resetting the operating system or, optionally, an individual process. Some test cases are REQUIRED and others OPTIONAL.

Before each test, the device must forward traffic for at least 15 seconds. The tester then triggers the reset and records frame loss or timestamps. For a power interruption, the loss of power lasts at least 15 seconds; the RFC says to subtract that 15-second interruption from the reported reset time to aid comparison.
sections.plainLanguage: The tests cover restarting hardware, restarting software, and removing power. Each test starts after the device has forwarded traffic, then measures when forwarding returns.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Benchmarking uses controlled traffic in a laboratory with dedicated address space. The test network MUST NOT connect to devices that could forward test traffic into a production network or misroute it to the management network.

The method measures the device from outside, as a black box. The RFC says there are no specific security considerations within its scope, while requiring that the test setup remain separate from production.
sections.plainLanguage: Run these tests on a separate lab network. Test traffic must not reach production equipment or the management network.
